analysis.one_liner: Requires safety standards and warning labels to keep furniture and TVs from tipping onto children.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 45 bipartisan cosponsors, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write mandatory safety standards for furniture and electronic appliances that can tip over, such as dressers, bookcases, and TV stands. Items that could not withstand tipping pressure would have to include anchoring devices and instructions, and packaging would carry warning labels telling parents to secure furniture to the wall. The bill was named for two children who died in furniture tip-overs, and it never got past its first House subcommittee.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with young children, who face the main risk: the bill's findings cite 8,000 to 10,000 emergency-room visits each year from furniture or appliance tip-overs, about 6 deaths per year, with most victims children. Consumers would also get clearer warnings and included anchoring hardware for furniture that cannot stay upright on its own.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the CPSC to set mandatory stability standards for any furniture or appliance it determines poses a substantial tipping hazard, replacing a field with no mandatory standards at all.

Requires anchoring devices, such as angle-braces and wall anchors, plus picture instructions to be included in the packaging of furniture that cannot pass the tipping test, so parents can secure it without buying extra hardware.

Requires clear warning labels on packaging stating that unsecured furniture can tip and cause serious injury or death, and that children can use drawers as steps, so buyers know the risk before the product enters the home.

analysis.who_pays: Furniture and electronic appliance manufacturers, which would bear the cost of redesigning or testing products to meet stability standards and adding anchoring hardware and warning labels to packaging. Some of that cost would likely pass through to consumers in slightly higher prices.

drawbacks.text: Manufacturers would bear real compliance costs for redesign, testing, anchors, and labels, and small furniture makers could feel them most; supporters of the bill would acknowledge some of this lands in consumer prices.

The bill delegates the core judgments to the CPSC — which products are hazardous and how much tipping pressure furniture must withstand — so the final rules could be narrower or broader than Congress intended, and the 180-day deadline for such rulemaking was ambitious.
Warning labels only inform people who read them; the standard's real protection depends on consumers actually installing the included anchors, which no label can guarantee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stakes are lopsided in one direction: the deaths at issue are a small number per year, but each is a child, the injuries number in the thousands annually, and the fix — stable design, a strap, a label — is cheap relative to the harm. The main honest counterweight is compliance cost for manufacturers and the risk that rulemaking drags. The bill's main weakness was not its design but that it never moved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and nothing further happened before the Congress ended — no hearing, no vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Allyson Schwartz introduced the bill on April 26, 2005, joined by Reps. McGovern and Davis of Illinois as original sponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction.
On May 13, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where the record ends.
The bill attracted 45 cosponsors, 42 Democrats and 3 Republicans, but the committee never acted on it during the 109th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Furniture and electronic appliance manufacturers came out ahead: no mandatory stability standards or labeling requirements were imposed, so they avoided redesign, testing, and packaging costs for another Congress.

for.name: Allyson Schwartz
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill naming mandatory furniture and appliance tip-over standards and warning labels.

for.name: 45 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support, giving the bill bipartisan backing it never converted into committee action.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX) at the time
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never reported the bill out; no markup, hearing action, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection
against.role: Subcommittee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 2005 onward; the record shows no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Democratic (42 of 45) but included 3 Republicans, and no recorded vote ever separated the parties; the bill died quietly in committee rather than through a partisan fight.

industries.note: The bill would have forced stability testing, redesign, and anchoring hardware in every box of qualifying furniture, ending a regime with no mandatory safety standards. Its interest in avoiding those costs ran against the safety of children in tip-over-prone homes.
TVs and electronic appliances the CPSC deemed tipping hazards would fall under the same standards and labeling rules. The category was growing in importance as large, heavy TVs entered more homes.
Retailers would stock safer, labeled products at somewhat higher prices; warning labels and included anchors could also reduce liability exposure from unsecured furniture.
